nameStory: The red sunflower gets its name from its vibrant reddish-orange petals that glow like flames, quite different from the classic yellow of common sunflowers. It's also called Mexican sunflower because it originally comes from Mexico and Central America, where it brightens tropical landscapes.
description: Red sunflower is a tall, bushy annual plant that can reach 4-6 feet high with broad, heart-shaped leaves and striking reddish-orange daisy-like flowers. Each flower head is about 2-3 inches across with bright orange-red petals surrounding a golden center. This tropical native is sometimes grown in New England gardens as an ornamental but rarely escapes cultivation due to our cooler climate.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Brilliant orange-red daisy-like blooms about 2-3 inches across with 8-13 broad petals surrounding a golden-yellow center disk that feels slightly fuzzy to the touch

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large, heart-shaped to triangular leaves that feel rough and sandpapery on top, with prominent veins and serrated edges; leaves alternate up the stem

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall, branching annual that grows 4-6 feet high with sturdy, hollow stems that feel thick and succulent when squeezed

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small, dark brown seeds with papery scales that develop in the center disk after flowers fade, easily scattered by wind

habitat: In New England, red sunflower is almost exclusively found in cultivated gardens, particularly those with well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Very rarely, you might spot an escaped plant near gardens or compost areas, but it cannot survive our winters and doesn't establish wild populations.

seasonality.spring: Seeds may be planted in gardens after last frost, but young plants won't be visible until late spring when soil warms sufficiently.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with continuous bright orange-red flowers from mid-summer through early fall, attracting butterflies and hummingbirds.
seasonality.fall: Continues blooming until first hard frost kills the plant; seeds mature and can be collected from dried flower heads.
seasonality.winter: Annual plant dies completely with frost; only persists as seeds that cannot survive New England winters outdoors.

funFact: Red sunflower flowers actually track the sun throughout the day just like their yellow cousins, slowly rotating their bright orange faces from east to west - a behavior called heliotropism that you can observe in real-time if you watch closely!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with orange cosmos or marigolds, but red sunflower's much larger size (4-6 feet tall), rough sandpapery leaves, and thick hollow stems quickly distinguish it from these shorter, more delicate flowers.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name, red sunflower isn't actually red but rather a vibrant orange-red color, and it's not closely related to the common sunflower we know for seeds - it belongs to a different genus entirely within the huge sunflower family.
compareHints: Red sunflower is the only Tithonia species found in New England gardens. Within the broader sunflower family, it differs from common sunflowers by its orange-red petals (not yellow), smaller flower heads, and much rougher, heart-shaped leaves rather than the oval, softer leaves of true sunflowers.
